To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the annual domain-average emissions of CO, NOx, and NH3 from the U.S transportation sector are projected to decrease by 2046- 2050, while the PM and SO2 emissions increase in some regions due to increases in emissions from ships.

1) transportation emissions are projected to decrease by 2046-50, 2) on-road and nonroad engines dominate the emission changes, 3) the WRF-CMAQ model is able to simulate meteorological and chemical variables with good performance, and 4) this modeling framework can be applied to investigate the impacts of projected emissions on air quality under climate change.

1) the Technology Driver Model is a useful tool that can be used to estimate future emissions of the U.S. transport sector, 2) the dynamically downscaled WRF/CMAQ modeling system can be used to simulate the baseline air quality, and 3) the Technology Driver model and the modeling system can be combined to simulate future air quality in the context of climate change.

the development and evaluation of an integrated modeling framework that will allow us to examine the impact of transportation emission changes on air quality and climate in the future.
the impacts of projected future emissions on U.S. air pollution, and the results of this study will be used to examine the air quality impacts of projected emissions in Part II.

the impact of projected transportation emissions in the face of a changing climate, and we provide an overview of the modeling framework and evaluation of the baseline simulations for Part II of this study.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the WRF/CMAQ system is able to capture the spatial and temporal variations in the baseline 2000s meteorology and air quality over the U.S. and is thus suitable to investigate future emission scenarios.
this study presents a novel methodology that can be used to assess the impact of future emissions from a specific sector (e.g., transportation) in the face of future climate change.
this study provides an important step toward understanding the impact of future U.S. transportation emissions on air quality in a warming climate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Technology Driver Model is capable of providing emission projections with high spatial and temporal resolution, and the dynamically downscaled WRF/CMAQ modeling system is capable of reproducing the meteorological and chemical variables with reasonable accuracy, thus providing a useful platform for Part II of this study.

we have successfully developed a Technology Driver Model and the associated emission projections for the future, and we have also configured/evaluated a dynamically downscaled WRF/CMAQ system for the future air quality simulations.
the emission projection methodology and model evaluation are both sound.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Technology Driver Model is a powerful tool to project future emissions from the transportation sector and the dynamically downscaled WRF/CMAQ system is capable of simulating the baseline meteorology and air quality well.

future emission projections are important for understanding future changes in air quality, and the WRF-CMAQ modeling system is capable of reproducing the current-day meteorology and air quality in the contiguous U.S. with reasonable confidence.

a dynamically downscaled modeling system can be used for future air quality simulations, and that such modeling system is a useful tool in understanding future air quality changes in the face the rapidly changing transportation sector and climate.
